prompt:
LAPTOP page, 1536x1024 first viewport, same masthead and margins as the reference. Show START HERE heading, the lede, then all three examples side by side.
DIRECTION B: the three examples as three equal ruled columns (REPORTER | NONPROFIT | RESIDENT), each column: label, big question, numbered steps, then its excerpt box below, Try it at the bottom; hairlines between columns.

Design system (keep exactly, from the reference screenshot of the sibling "How it works" page): "The Rundown" newsroom rundown sheet. White paper #ffffff, ink #111111, light gray band #ededea, graphite #5c5c5c for secondary text. Masthead: the heavy condensed wordmark CREAM CITY ALMANAC; on laptops the site links SEARCH  ASK  SAVED, then START HERE and HOW IT WORKS set apart; START HERE is the current page (ink, underlined by a thick ink bar). Headings in bold condensed newsroom capitals (Saira Extra Condensed 700); body in a plain sans (Vazirmatn). Thin black rules, flat ruled boxes, small boxed provenance tags like [AI] [DYCU] [HUB]. No shadows, no rounded corners, no cards, no color except ink and gray. Red #d7261e only as a hand-drawn grease-pencil mark, if at all.

Page content, in this order (real words; use them verbatim):
- Heading "START HERE"; lede "Three people, three questions, and how each gets an answer here."
- Example 1. Label "A REPORTER". Question in large type: "Do the neighborhoods with the most old housing also have the most asthma?" Numbered steps: 1 Search older housing and asthma rates. Asthma Prevalence and Housing Built Before 1950 come up. 2 Read each sheet's caveats first: they say what the numbers can and can't support. 3 Use the story angles as starting questions. 4 Download both CSVs and match them by census tract. Excerpt box: small label "H05 story angles", two bullets "Which Milwaukee-area neighborhoods have the largest shares of older housing, and what does that mean for repair needs and housing costs? [AI]" and "Are areas with older housing stock also areas where residents face higher housing burdens or maintenance problems? [AI]"; small label "W01 caveat", "These are modeled estimates produced by a methodology, not direct counts of people with asthma, so avoid saying how many people have asthma. [AI]". Link "Try it →".
- Example 2. Label "A NONPROFIT". Question: "Our grant application needs Harambee's poverty numbers, by age." Steps: 1 Open the Neighborhood Portrait Spreadsheet (N03). 2 Pick Harambee and the newest year, then Poverty Status by Age. 3 Quote each estimate with its margin of error, and cite the Census table linked on the sheet. 4 For the story behind the numbers, read Harambee's Neighborhood Portrait report. Excerpt: a hairline-boxed note "Percentages and precision columns have formula errors in DYCU's file, so they aren't shown."; a small ruled table captioned "Harambee, 2024: Poverty Status by Age" with columns Estimate | ± Margin and rows "Total 18,894 ±1,504", "Income in the past 12 months below poverty level 6,520 ±790", "Under 5 years 608 ±252"; then "[DYCU] Census table B17001". Link "Try it →".
- Example 3. Label "A RESIDENT". Question: "What has the air been like in Milwaukee lately?" Steps: 1 Search air quality and open Daily Air Quality (V02). 2 The live preview charts every day's reading, straight from DYCU's Hub. No download needed. 3 Read the caveat before comparing days or years. Excerpt: a small strip chart of daily AQI readings, one thin ink strip per year (2023, 2024, 2025), plus "Each value is a citywide daily average of sensor readings, so it can hide differences between neighborhoods. [AI]". Link "Try it →".
- Section "DYCU'S OWN GUIDES": three links each followed by [HUB]: Getting Started, About the Data, Questions and Feedback; then "Questions about the data itself: hub@datayoucanuse.org".
- Last line: "How the almanac works →".
approvedRole: laptop: the three examples as three ruled columns
